title: Ebola Has Passed 1,000 Cases. This Outbreak Is Different From Any Before
snippet:
The Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 1,000 confirmed Ebola cases by June 21, 2026, marking the first time since the 2018-2020 epidemic. This outbreak is particularly alarming as it's caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), for which no approved vaccine exists, rendering the Zaire strain vaccine ineffective. Spreading through remote, conflict-affected areas and now into Uganda, the current trajectory is significantly worse than previous outbreaks at similar stages, with no visible [...] Cumulative reported cases for three Ebola outbreaks on a logarithmic scale, each aligned to the day of official declaration. Solid lines show laboratory-confirmed cases; dashed lines include all reported cases (confirmed, probable and suspected); shaded regions reflect case classification uncertainty. The 2026 DRC/Uganda outbreak (magenta) had passed 1,000 confirmed cases by day 37 with no sign of slowing. Sources: WHO situation reports compiled by Caitlin Rivers (2014–2016), Kristian G. [...] The 2026 curve does neither. At day 37 from declaration, the 2026 outbreak had accumulated roughly ten times as many confirmed cases as the 2018–2020 outbreak at the same point. The slope shows no visible flattening. With 267 confirmed deaths, the case fatality rate sits near 25% — lower than 2018–2020, which likely reflects differences in surveillance completeness as much as anything about the virus itself.

The highly contagious Bundibugyo virus is relatively unfamiliar, but it killed around 30 per cent of infected persons in the two previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, respectively in Uganda and DRC. [...] The Ebola outbreak that was declared in eastern DRC on 15 May is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record. The Bundibugyo virus variant is less common and there is no approved vaccine or treatment. [...] The disease starts with flu-like symptoms including fever which can mask its true identity. Full-blown Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus is marked by severe bleeding and a fatality rate of around 40 per cent.
